title: De lineis curvis non in eodem plano sitis, quae maximi minimive proprietate sunt praeditae

deep.reconstruction:
Problem I of E740 asks for the space curve x ↦ (y(x), z(x)) that makes ∫ x dy dz/dx = ∫ x p q dx stationary, with p = y′ and q = z′. Euler sets V = pqx, so M = pq, N = N′ = 0, P = qx, P′ = px, and S = V − Pp − P′q = −pqx.

The two Euler–Lagrange equations 0 = d(qx) and 0 = d(px) say that y and z are cyclic variables. They integrate to qx = a and px = b. Hence q = np with n = a/b, and x = b/p, dx = −b dp/p².

Then dy = p dx = −b dp/p, giving y = f − b ln p, and dz = q dx = −nb dp/p, giving z = g − nb ln p. Substituting p = b/x gives y = f − b ln b + b ln x. Absorbing the constant, y = f + b ln x and z = g + nb ln x. So both projections (on the xy and xz planes) are logarithmic curves.

§14 is a count of constants. The general solution has four arbitrary constants f, g, n, b, as required by two second-order equations.

§15 eliminates x to get z = ny + c, so the projection on the plane BOC (the yz plane) is a straight line. The whole extremal therefore lies in a plane, namely the vertical plane z = ny + c containing the x direction. Euler observes that the example strictly falls outside his topic (non-planar curves). He adds that it shows how the method reveals when the solution happens to be planar.

The redundant third equation M dx = dS, the Beltrami/energy-type identity, checks out: pq = ab/x² and d(pqx) = d(ab/x) = −ab dx/x², so pq dx = −d(pqx). This holds identically, consistent with Euler's remark on the previous page that it follows from the other two.
errors: Euler does not discuss whether the extremal is a maximum or a minimum. The Hessian of V with respect to (p, q) is [[0, x], [x, 0]], which is indefinite, so the Legendre condition fails. The extremal is a saddle-type stationary curve, neither a maximum nor a minimum. This is a gap in interpretation, not in calculation, and is typical of the period.

ideas.what: Euler–Lagrange equations for two dependent functions y(x), z(x) (curve in space), with a cyclic-variable first integral
ideas.modern_name: Euler–Lagrange system for several unknown functions; conserved momenta for cyclic coordinates

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine worked example: the Euler–Lagrange equations with cyclic variables give logarithmic projections and a planar extremal. Euler himself flags it as degenerate. Nothing here goes beyond standard calculus of variations as it stood around 1780.
transcription_corrections: The transcription matches the image. 'blb' and 'blx' denote b·log b and b·log x (Euler writes l for the logarithm).
